analysis.one_liner: Lets people wipe out private student loans in bankruptcy like other debts.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it sat in the Senate Judiciary Committee for the entire two-year Congress and expired there, despite 16 cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current bankruptcy law, almost no student loan can be wiped out unless the borrower proves that repaying it would cause "undue hardship" — a very high bar. This bill would keep that hard rule for federal and government-backed student loans but remove it for private student loans from banks and lenders, letting a judge treat those like credit card debt or medical debt. It was introduced by Sen. Durbin with 16 cosponsors and referred to the Judiciary Committee, which never acted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: People overwhelmed by private student loan debt — typically borrowers who attended for-profit or vocational schools or whose loans carry high interest rates. In bankruptcy they could ask a judge to cancel the private portion of their student debt, the same relief already available for credit cards, medical bills, and gambling debts. Their families benefit too, since wages, homes, and retirement savings currently at risk to satisfy an undischargeable loan would be protected.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Borrowers drowning in private student loans

how_it_helps.text: Makes privately issued student loans dischargeable in bankruptcy, ending the special rule that currently shields them the way government-backed loans are shielded.
Keeps the existing 'undue hardship' rule for loans made, insured, or guaranteed by a government, so the change is targeted at private lenders only.
A borrower who qualifies would no longer have to prove 'undue hardship' — a standard most debtors cannot meet — to have a judge cancel private loan debt.

analysis.who_pays: Private student loan lenders, such as banks and specialty lenders like Sallie Mae. They would lose the legal guarantee — added in 2005 — that their loans survive bankruptcy, so some loans they now expect to collect in full would instead be discharged, and they would likely price that risk into rates or tighten lending standards.

drawbacks.text: Lenders and defenders of the current rule argue that the 2005 protection keeps private student credit available and rates lower, because lenders can recover even from borrowers who later file for bankruptcy; removing it could raise rates or reduce loan access for some students.

Supporters of the stricter rule worry that recent graduates with strong future earnings could file for bankruptcy to escape loans shortly after leaving school, shifting costs to lenders and other borrowers.
The bill does nothing for borrowers whose debts are federal loans, which are the majority of student debt and would remain subject to the same undue-hardship bar as today.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For borrowers with unpayable private student loans, the relief is substantial and targeted: the change applies only to private loans, so federal loan programs and taxpayers are untouched. The real cost falls on private lenders, who accepted it as a business risk debate; the main good-faith concern is that easier discharge could raise private loan rates for future students, though private student loans were routinely dischargeable before 2005 and the market functioned. The bill was a narrow, targeted fix rather than a broad reworking of bankruptcy law.

outcome.mechanism: It was read twice and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never held a hearing or vote, so the bill died when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Sen. Durbin introduced the bill on January 23, 2013, joined by Sens. Whitehouse, Franken, Harkin, Reed, and Warren as original cosponsors.
Sixteen senators cosponsored the bill: 15 Democrats and 1 Independent; no Republican cosponsored.
The bill's only action after introduction was being read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary on January 23, 2013.
The Judiciary Committee took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the remainder of the 113th Congress, which ended January 3, 2015.
This was a repeat effort: Durbin had introduced versions of the same bankruptcy fix in earlier Congresses, and none became law.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private student loan lenders came out ahead: their loans remain shielded from bankruptcy discharge, and they avoided any risk that a judge could cancel their debts. The committee system also meant no senator ever had to go on record for or against the bill.

for.name: Sen. Richard Durbin
for.role: U.S. Senator from Illinois; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led it; had carried versions of the same fix in earlier Congresses.

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including original cosponsors Whitehouse, Franken, Harkin, Reed, and Warren.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee (chaired by Sen. Patrick Leahy)
against.what_they_did: Accepted the referral but never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote; the bill expired in committee.

against.name: Private student loan lenders
against.role: Industry whose loans the bill would make dischargeable
against.what_they_did: Opposed earlier versions of this same proposal and defended the 2005 bankruptcy protection for their loans.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred, so there is no roll call to measure; all 16 cosponsors were Democrats or an Independent and no Republican signed on, but no senator ever voted against the bill on the record.

industries.industry: Private student loan lenders (banks and specialty lenders like Sallie Mae and Nelnet)
industries.note: Since 2005, private student loans have been nearly impossible to discharge in bankruptcy, making them among the safest debts a lender can hold — a borrower's future income is collateral whether the degree pays off or not. The bill would strip that protection for private loans only, meaning some loans now collected in full would instead be cancelled in bankruptcy.
Government-issued and government-backed loans would keep their existing 'undue hardship' discharge rule, unchanged. The bill is written so federal lending and taxpayers are not affected.
